title.analysis: Authentic title "8 Things That Are a Complete WASTE of Your Money" is a numbered-list warning frame. The script delivers eight items (warranties, subscriptions, overdraft fees, lottery, card interest, sports betting, investment fees, car debt) with a running composite household tally, so the promise is kept.

White background: the recurring cartoon man, angry, pointing at a trash can; "STOP BUYING THESE!" in heavy black capitals; the can holds a Starbucks-branded cup, an iPhone, a red shopping bag, sneakers, a T-shirt, a game controller and a Bitcoin coin, with a red X. script.stored_text_completeness: All 19281 canonical characters read sequentially in full in 1 bounded ranges; auto-generated untimed text; stored text ends mid-sentence ("because I read those and honestly they're the best") with no sign-off, so the ending is truncated; ASR garbles include "986,000 a year" (the household income is later 96,000), "1666 billion", "20 1,600", "30 360" and the composite name rendered as Dileia/Dia; the investment-fee tally item reads "250" although 1.15% of $180,000 is $2,070; audio, timed delivery and editing unverified.
script.opening_words: Two trucks in the same lot, 40 feet apart. One guy's here at 4:40 in the morning because he has to be. The other one's here because he wanted a bagel. They apprenticed together 31 years ago, 4 months apart in age, and neither household has ever pulled ahead of the other by more than a rounding error. 986,000 a year. Probably not far off yours. The bagel guy stopped at 62. He's got a boat that is objectively not
script.ending_words: you drive because you want a bagel and the truck you drive because you have to. Go be the bagel guy. One last reminder, this is educational only and none of it is advice. Every result depends on your own decisions and your own numbers. Go run them. Then tell me in the comments which of these eight you're killing first because I read those and honestly they're the best
script.analysis: Full 19281 canonical characters read. A single-narrator narrative listicle with two framing devices (two tradesmen with equal incomes, and a composite couple, Dileia and Reuben, on $96,000): eight items, each with a mechanism and a dollar figure, a running tally, a $10,000-a-year total compounded to about $946,000, an emotional passage, a regulatory-rollback reframe (overdraft cap, click-to-cancel, late-fee cap), a faceless-YouTube community promotion, and a callback close. Regulatory history is accurate; several calculations are not: the fee-drag gap uses a 20-year figure for 30 years, the tally sums to $8,215 as spoken, and the minimum-payment example does not reproduce.
